4901004550				CC_BY_NC_4_0	2024-06-27T15:15:38Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222494234	hussain niyaz					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HUMAN_OBSERVATION	Coordinate uncertainty increased to 31350m to protect threatened taxon			https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/222494234	222494234		hussain niyaz															PRESENT								Sri Lankan elephant during my visit to Yala National Park. These gentle giants are not just a symbol of Sri Lanka’s rich wildlife heritage but also play a crucial role in the island's ecosystem. Yala National Park, along with Bundala National Park, offers a haven for these elephants, providing them with a safe and natural habitat. Observing them in the wild is truly a humbling experience, showcasing their strength, intelligence, and the serene beauty of nature. The Sri Lankan elephant (Elephas maximus maximus) is a subspecies of the Asian elephant, native to Sri Lanka. These elephants are known for their distinct physical characteristics, including a relatively large body size and prominent depigmentation patches on their ears, face, trunk, and belly. Conservation efforts are vital for their survival, as they face threats from habitat loss and human-elephant conflict. taxon			https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/17761405	17761405		subiksha															PRESENT								"Scientific and Common Name: The scientific name of this organism is Elephas maximus ssp. maximus.⁷ This organism is commonly known as the Sri Lankan elephants and are subspecies of the Asian elephants.¹¹ Habitat and Geographic Range: Sri Lankan elephants are exclusively found in Sri Lanka.¹¹ At one point in time, they were found all throughout Sri Lanka,¹ however, they are now being forced into small areas in the north, east, and southeast regions¹⁰ away from their migratory routes.¹¹As stated by the World Wildlife Fund, the elephants are found in biomes such as, ""the tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests, and the tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests"", and the corresponding ecological regions are, ""tropical evergreen forest, semi-evergreen forest, moist deciduous forest, dry deciduous forest, and dry thorn forest"".¹¹ The vegetation in the forests are found in tall trees, out of the elephant's reach, thus, there are low elephant densities in those areas.² In contrast, there are high densities in areas with more light, grass and pioneer species along river courses.² In addition, Sri Lankan elephants do not migrate to other areas as their home ranges are related to their fitness.² Size/Weight and Lifespan: Sri Lankan elephants are the largest subspecies of the Asian elephants, and the body weight and height of the male elephants are larger than the female elephants.⁵ The average weight of an adult female is 2588 kg, and the average shoulder height ranges from 220 to 240 cm.⁵ The average weight of an adult male is 4589 kg, and the average shoulder height ranges from 240 to 260 cm.⁵ Only 2% of the total population have tusks; and males have longer tusks than females.¹⁰ The average lifespan of the Sri Lankan elephants in the wild is around 60 years of age.⁸ Diet: The Sri Lankan elephants are one of the few mammals who are mega-herbivores.⁴ Due to their enormous body weight, they have a great physiological demand for a large and high energy diet.⁴ A daily food consumption of about 10% of their body weight is required, thus, they have evolved to be generalist herbivores.² The type of plants they consume are dependent upon the different habitats and seasons they live in.⁴ Sri Lankan elephants in particular, feed on over a hundred different species of vegetation² including, grass, roots, fruit, sugar cane¹¹ and bark.⁸ In Sri Lanka, grass is highly abundant and is considered to be the primary food source.² During the dry seasons, the elephants raid crops that contain high in nutrition pioneer species which are repeatedly harvested and are available in abundance.² In addition, elephants have evolved to develop thick skin and a tolerant digestive tract lining, in order to consume plants with thorns.² Reproduction and Communication: Sri Lankan elephants have sexually dimorphic traits, with the males being larger than the females.² There is male-male competition in order to attain a receptive female, and the winning male will guard the female during her fertile period.² The receptive female secretes pheromones in urine or feces, which attracts other males during her ovulation period.² The female elephants on average reach sexual maturity around 10 to 16 years of age, and they give birth around 12 to 18 years of age.⁶ The females have a gestation period of about 2 years (22 months),⁶ and the females come into oestrus once every 4 to 5 years.² Moreover, in a research paper published in 2010,⁹ the researchers observed over 400 female Sri Lankan elephants and identified 14 distinct call types; 8 calls were single calls, and 5 were combination calls.⁹ The acoustic signals varied among different social contexts, age, and sex classes.⁹ Growls and rumbles where heard when the elephants oriented towards and object of attention.⁹ Bark, roars and long roars occurred during periods of separation, movement, searching, distress, and high arousal.⁹ Squeaks, squeals, and trumpets were heard in response to disturbance.⁹ Predation: The top animal predator in Sri Lanka is known to be the leopard, however, it does not pose a threat to the Sri Lankan adult elephants nor the calves, due to their large body sizes.³ However, most of the threats to Sri Lankan elephants are from humans, and in particular, through poaching of ivory, leather and elephant meat.⁴ The long-term survival of these elephants can be compromised by poaching, as it changes adult sex ratios resulting in a highly female biased population, and reduces genetic variation, fertility and recruitment.⁴ In addition, large-scale hunting of meat and hides significantly reduce populations as this activity results in death.⁴ Conservation Status: According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature,⁴ Sri Lankan Elephants are considered to be endangered, and ""they have a high risk of facing extinction in the wild.""¹¹ The population has decreased about 65% since the 19th century,¹¹ however, the Sri Lankan elephants are currently protected by the Sri Lankan Law, and conservation efforts are in place.¹¹
